---
title: dropnests
---
## Drop Redundant Nesting {.unnumbered}


### Description

<code>dropnests()</code> drops redundant nesting of a list. <br />
It is the hierarchical equivalent to the dimensional drop function. <br />
<br />



### Usage

<pre><code class='language-R'>dropnests(x, ...)

## Default S3 method:
dropnests(x, maxdepth = 16L, recurse_classed = FALSE, ...)
</code></pre>


### Arguments

<table>
<tr><td style = "white-space: collapse; font-family: monospace; vertical-align: top"><code id="x">x</code></td>
<td>
a list
</td></tr>
<tr><td style = "white-space: collapse; font-family: monospace; vertical-align: top"><code id="...">...</code></td>
<td>
further arguments passed to or from methods. <br /> <br />
</td></tr>
<tr><td style = "white-space: collapse; font-family: monospace; vertical-align: top"><code id="maxdepth">maxdepth</code></td>
<td>
a single, positive integer, giving the maximum depth to drop nesting in. <br />
The surface-level elements of a list is depth 1;
so when <code>maxdepth = 1</code>, <code>x</code> will be returned unchanged.
</td></tr>
<tr><td style = "white-space: collapse; font-family: monospace; vertical-align: top"><code id="recurse_classed">recurse_classed</code></td>
<td>
<code>TRUE</code> or <code>FALSE</code>,
indicating if the function should also recurse through classed lists within <code>x</code>,
like data.frames.
</td></tr>
</table>


### Value

A flattened list,
with names that indicate the original dimensional positions of the elements. <br />
<br />



### Examples
```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = NA}
library("broadcast")


x <- list(
  list(list(list(list(1:10)))),
  list(1:10)
)
print(x)

dropnests(x)


```
